tips: Read the question stem first so you know what you are looking for in the source.

Separate evidence (what the text says) from inference (what you conclude from it).

G12.title: Leaving Haran (Genesis 12:1–4)
G12.attr: Genesis 12:1–4, as printed in your Lesson 1.4 source sheet.
G12.label: From your class packet.
paras: 1. G-d said to Avram, "Go forth from your land, from your birthplace and from your father's house to the land that I will show you.
2. I will make of you a great nation, and I will bless you; I will make your name great, and you shall be a blessing.
3. I will bless those who bless you … and all the families of the earth shall bless themselves by you."
4. So Avram went, as G-d had spoken to him, and Lot went with him.

G13.title: Avraham and Lot (Genesis 13:7–11)
G13.attr: Genesis 13, as printed in your Lesson 1.4 source sheet.
G13.label: From your class packet.
paras: 7. There was quarreling between the herdsmen of Avram and the herdsmen of Lot.
8. Avram said to Lot, "Let there be no quarrel between you and me, and between my herdsmen and yours, for we are relatives.
9. Is not the whole land before you? Please separate from me. If you go to the left, I will go to the right; and if you go to the right, I will go to the left."
10–11. Lot looked out, chose the well-watered Jordan plain for himself, and the two separated.

G16.title: Hagar (Genesis 16:1–6)
G16.attr: Genesis 16, as printed in your Lesson 1.4 source sheet.
G16.label: From your class packet.
paras: Sarai said to Avram, "G-d has kept me from bearing. Consort with my servant; perhaps I shall have a son through her." And Avram listened to Sarai.
He came to Hagar and she conceived; and when she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was lowered in her esteem.
Sarai said to Avram, "The wrong done me is your fault! … Let G-d decide between you and me!"
Avram said to Sarai, "Your servant is in your hands; do to her as you think best." Then Sarai treated her harshly, and Hagar ran away from her.

G18.title: Avraham pleads for Sodom (Genesis 18:23–25)
G18.attr: Genesis 18, as printed in your Avraham text study.
G18.label: From your class packet.
G18.text: Abraham came forward and said, "Will You indeed sweep away the innocent along with the guilty? What if there should be fifty innocent within the city; will You then wipe out the place and not forgive it for the sake of the innocent fifty who are in it? Far be it from You to do such a thing, to bring death upon the innocent as well as the guilty, so that innocent and guilty fare alike. Far be it from You! Shall not the Judge of all the earth deal justly?"

G22.title: Akeidat Yitzchak (Genesis 22:1–3, 7–8)
G22.attr: Genesis 22, as printed in your Lesson 1.4 source sheet.
G22.label: From your class packet.
paras: G-d tested Avraham and said to him, "Avraham," and he answered, "Here I am." G-d said, "Take your son, your favored one, Yitzchak, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering…"
So early the next morning, Avraham saddled his donkey … and set out for the place of which G-d had told him.

Yitzchak said, "Father! … Here are the firestone and the wood; but where is the sheep for the burnt offering?" Avraham said, "G-d will see to the sheep for the burnt offering, my son." And the two of them walked on together.

BR.title: The palace (Bereishit Rabbah 39:1)
BR.attr: Midrash compiled c. 5th century CE, as printed in "Avraham: Why Was He Chosen?"
BR.label: From your class packet.
BR.text: A man was traveling when he saw a beautifully illuminated palace. He wondered, 'Is it possible that this palace has no owner?' Immediately the owner looked out and said, 'I am the owner of this palace.' Likewise, Avraham looked at the world and wondered, 'Is it possible that this world has no One who governs it?' Immediately G-d revealed Himself to Avraham.

RAM.title: Rambam on Avraham
RAM.attr: Rambam (Maimonides), Mishneh Torah, Laws of Foreign Worship 1:3, as printed in "Avraham: Why Was He Chosen?"
RAM.label: From your class packet.
RAM.text: After this mighty man was weaned, he began to explore and think. Though he was a child he began to think incessantly … wondering: how is it possible for the sphere to continue to revolve without having anyone controlling it? Who is causing it to revolve? … He had no teacher… Rather he was mired in Ur Kasdim among the foolish idolaters… He realized that there was one G-d who controlled the sphere, that He created everything, and that there is no other G-d among all the other entities… Abraham was forty years old when he became aware of his Creator.

UR.title: Ur and southern Mesopotamia
UR.attr: From the evidence packet "Should He Leave Mesopotamia?" (Source C).
UR.label: From your class packet.
paras: Ur was one of the important cities of ancient Mesopotamia and was part of a highly developed urban civilization.
The Tigris and Euphrates river system supported irrigation. Canals moved water to fields and helped farmers produce grain and other crops.
Ur participated in long-distance trade. Because southern Mesopotamia lacked some natural resources, merchants imported materials such as timber, metals, and stone.
Wealthy households could own livestock, goods, land-use rights, and valuable possessions and could depend on extended family and business relationships.

questions.stem: Which statement is directly stated in the passage rather than inferred?
options: Avram felt no fear about leaving home
Avram went as G-d had spoken
Avram wanted to become a great nation
Avram trusted G-d more than his own family
questions.exp: Verse 4 states the action. Fear, wishes and trust are inferences.
why: The text records his action, not his feelings.
The text gives G-d's promise, not Avram's wishes.

questions.stem: The Torah most likely lists 'your land, your birthplace and your father's house' in order to
options: show that Avram owned three separate homes
explain where the land of Canaan was located
show that Lot had to leave all three as well
stress how much Avram was asked to give up
questions.exp: Three layers of home make the request heavier.
why: The list is about attachments, not property.
The destination isn't named at all.
The command is spoken to Avram.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about the relationship in the passage is best supported?
options: Both sides take on commitments
Only Avram is bound by any obligation
Only G-d is bound by any obligation
Neither side expects anything from the other
questions.exp: Avram must leave; G-d promises nation, blessing, a great name.

questions.stem: Which quality is best supported by Avram's words to Lot?
options: Fear of fighting his nephew
Desire for the best land
Putting peace before advantage
Obedience to a command from G-d
questions.exp: "Let there be no quarrel… for we are relatives."
why: The text stresses peace among relatives, not fear.
No command from G-d appears here.

questions.stem: Compared with Genesis 12:4, Avraham's behavior in this passage is best described as
options: obeying silently and without question, just as in Genesis 12
protecting his own household from harm
challenging G-d rather than simply obeying
refusing to speak with G-d at all
questions.exp: Genesis 12: he goes. Genesis 18: he argues for justice.
why: He argues for strangers in Sodom.

questions.stem: Which claim does Avraham make in the passage?
options: The innocent should not die with the guilty
Everyone living in the city of Sodom is innocent of any wrongdoing
G-d has no authority over the city
Lot's family alone deserves to be saved
questions.exp: His appeal is to justice for the innocent.
why: He asks about fifty innocent among the guilty.
He calls G-d 'Judge of all the earth.'

questions.stem: A student claims, 'Avraham always stood up for people who were vulnerable.' Which detail best challenges this claim?
options: "Will You sweep away the innocent?"
"Let there be no quarrel between us"
"G-d has kept me from bearing"
"Your servant is in your hands"
questions.exp: With Hagar, he hands the conflict back to Sarai, and Hagar flees.
why: That supports the claim; it's from Sodom.
That shows peacemaking, not a failure to protect.
Sarai says this; it's not about Avraham's choices.

questions.stem: Which detail most directly shows Avraham acted without delay?
options: He told Yitzchak that G-d would provide
He set out early the next morning
He answered 'Here I am' when called
The two of them walked on together
questions.exp: "So early the next morning, Avraham saddled his donkey."
why: That shows faith or reassurance, not timing.
That shows readiness to listen, not timing of action.

questions.stem: According to the midrash, who takes the first step?
options: G-d calls Avraham with no prior search
Avraham asks; then G-d answers
The palace owner searches for the traveler
Neither one acts until Sinai
questions.exp: This supports 'they chose each other.'
why: That fits Genesis 12, not this midrash.

questions.stem: How does Rambam's account differ from Genesis 12?
options: It says Avraham was born in Canaan
It says Avraham had a great teacher
It says G-d spoke to Avraham as a baby
It explains why Avraham was chosen
questions.exp: Genesis 12 gives no reason; Rambam fills the gap with Avraham's search.
why: Rambam says he had no teacher.

questions.stem: What is the strongest reason to be careful using Rambam as evidence of what Avraham thought?
options: He wrote many centuries after Avraham
He disagreed with the Torah about where Avraham was born
He never wrote about Avraham at all
He was one of the idolaters in Ur
questions.exp: A later interpreter fills gaps; he is not an eyewitness.
why: He places Avraham in Ur, as tradition does.
He lived much later, in the Middle Ages.

questions.stem: Which detail from this source would a wealthy household in Ur most likely use to argue for staying?
options: Canaan's seasonal rainfall
Imported timber, metals and stone
Family and business networks
The dangers of drought in Canaan
questions.exp: Staying keeps an established life and relationships.
why: That isn't in this source, and it describes Canaan, not Ur.

G46.title: Jacob's household (Genesis 46:26–27)
G46.label: From your class packet.
G46.text: All the persons belonging to Jacob who came to Egypt — his own issue aside from the wives of Jacob's sons — all these persons numbered 66. And Joseph's sons who were born to him in Egypt were two in number. Thus the total of Jacob's household who came to Egypt was 70 persons.

EX1.title: A new king (Exodus 1:6–10)
EX1.label: From your class packet.
paras: Joseph died, and all his brothers, and all that generation. But the Israelites were fertile and prolific; they multiplied and increased very greatly, so that the land was filled with them.

A new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph. And he said to his people, 'Look, the Israelite people are far too numerous for us. Let us deal shrewdly with them, so that they may not increase; otherwise in the event of war, they may join our enemies in fighting against us and rise from the ground.'

G47.title: Settling in Goshen (Genesis 45:10; 47:27)
G47.attr: Genesis 45 and 47, as printed in Lesson 2.2.
G47.label: From your class packet.
paras: "You will dwell in the region of Goshen where you will be near me — you and your children and your grandchildren, your flocks and your herds and all that is yours." (45:10)
"Thus Israel settled in the country of Egypt in the region of Goshen; they acquired holdings in it, and were fertile and increased greatly." (47:27)

G50.title: Joseph's last words (Genesis 50:20–25)
G50.label: From your class packet.
G50.text: "Besides, although you intended me harm, G-d intended it for good, so as to bring about the present result — the survival of many people…" So Joseph and his father's household remained in Egypt… At length, Joseph said to his brothers, 'I am about to die. G-d will surely take notice of you and bring you up from this land to the land G-d promised on oath to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob.' So Joseph made the sons of Israel swear, saying, 'When G-d has taken notice of you, you shall carry up my bones from here.'

SIN.title: Sinai and after (Exodus 19, Exodus 24, Deuteronomy 27)
SIN.attr: As printed in Lesson 2.3 "From Family to Nation."
SIN.label: From your class packet.
paras: "Now, therefore, if you obey my voice faithfully and keep my Covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples … you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." (Exodus 19:5–6)
"All the people answered with one voice, saying: 'Everything that the Lord has spoken we will do' … They said, 'Everything that the Lord has spoken we will do and obey.'" (Exodus 24:3, 7)

"Be silent, Israel, and listen. This day you have become the people of the Lord your G-d. Therefore, obey the Lord your G-d and follow His commandments and decrees." (Deuteronomy 27:9–10, forty years later)

questions.stem: Using your class definitions, the group in Genesis 46 is best described as
options: a nation with land and laws
a family
a people feared by Pharaoh
a kingdom of priests at Sinai
questions.exp: "All the persons belonging to Jacob": 70 people, three generations.
why: They have no land or government of their own.

questions.stem: What changes between the language of Genesis 46 and Exodus 1:9?
options: From 'slaves' to 'free people'
From 'a nation with laws' to 'a small family of seventy'
From 'Egyptians' to 'Canaanites'
From 'persons of Jacob' to 'the Israelite people'
questions.exp: Outsiders now see a distinct people.
why: They become slaves after this, not before.

questions.stem: According to Pharaoh, what is the cause of his plan to 'deal shrewdly' with the Israelites?
options: Their numbers and possible disloyalty in war
Their refusal to farm the land of Goshen as Joseph had ordered
Joseph's order that they leave Egypt
Their worship of the gods of Egypt
questions.exp: "Far too numerous… they may join our enemies."
why: Joseph has died; no such order.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Pharaoh's point of view in the passage?
options: He sees the Israelites as honored guests
He sees the Israelites as a small family
He sees growth as a security threat
He sees the Israelites as Egypt's rulers
questions.exp: The new king 'did not know Joseph.'
why: That was the earlier welcome under Joseph.
He fears them; he doesn't call them rulers.

questions.stem: Which detail best explains why leaving Egypt might have been difficult?
options: Pharaoh had already enslaved them
Goshen was far from Joseph
They acquired holdings and grew
They owned nothing in Egypt
questions.exp: Prosperity is a practical reason to stay.

questions.stem: What did Joseph most likely believe about when the Israelites should leave Egypt?
options: When G-d took notice of them
Right after the famine ended
Only after Pharaoh asked them to go
Never, since Egypt was the promised land
questions.exp: Pakod yifkod: 'G-d will surely take notice of you.'
why: He links leaving to G-d's action.
He names the land promised to Abraham.

questions.stem: Joseph's words connect most directly to which earlier promise?
options: Pharaoh's promise to feed the world
Lot's choice of the Jordan plain
The promise that Hagar's son would become a great nation
The land promised to Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov
questions.exp: He names Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

questions.stem: Which detail best shows Joseph expected a future return to Canaan?
options: "You intended me harm"
"Carry up my bones from here"
"The survival of many people"
"Joseph and his father's household remained"
questions.exp: He wants his bones taken to the promised land.
why: That explains why he came to Egypt.

questions.stem: Which is the clearest difference between Exodus 19:5–6 and G-d's words to Avram in Genesis 12?
options: Sinai removes all of G-d's promises
Sinai adds 'if' conditions for a whole people
Sinai is spoken to one man alone
Sinai happens before Avram ever leaves his father's house in Haran
questions.exp: "If you obey my voice … you shall be…"
why: Sinai includes promises such as 'treasured possession.'
It is spoken to the Children of Israel.

questions.stem: Why was it significant that the people answered 'with one voice'?
options: It showed the laws were forced on them
It meant only Moshe agreed
It showed they rejected the laws
They accepted the covenant together
questions.exp: A shared choice is a step from family to nation.

questions.stem: Why might Moshe tell a new generation 'this day you have become the people of the Lord'?
options: Each generation must accept the covenant itself
The covenant made at Sinai had been cancelled after the golden calf
They had already conquered the land
They had never heard of the covenant
questions.exp: Nationhood is renewed, not just inherited.
why: He is renewing it, not introducing it.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by all three excerpts together?
options: They became a nation only once they had settled in Canaan
They never accepted the covenant
They were treated as a nation before entering the land
The covenant belonged only to Moshe
questions.exp: Your answer: the land completed nationhood but didn't create it.
why: Two excerpts call them a nation or people in the wilderness.

RH.title: Rosh Hashanah traditions
RH.attr: From "Unpacked for Education: Rosh Hashanah Traditions," as highlighted in your copy.
RH.label: From your class packet.
paras: Beta Israel developed in relative isolation from the rabbinic Jewish communities of Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. As a result, many customs that now seem nearly universal — including apples and honey and the elaborate Rosh Hashanah seder — weren't historically central to Ethiopian Jewish practice.

Following the teachings of Rabbi Chaim Palachi … of Izmir, families worried that unfiltered honey might contain pieces of bees, which aren't kosher. Instead, they dipped apples into sugar, preserving the wish for sweetness without using honey.

Although both communities drew on ingredients such as coconut, cardamom and tropical fruit, Bene Israel and Cochin Jewish cuisines aren't interchangeable. Each adapted the holiday to the ingredients and cooking traditions of its own region.

WWS.title: What would you save?
WWS.attr: From "What Would You Save? Rebuilding Jewish Life," your two-day assignment.
WWS.label: From your class packet.
paras: A Torah scroll is valuable, but someone must know how to read it. A Jewish calendar identifies holidays, but people must understand how to observe them.

But knowledge alone is not enough. Communities also need institutions. Jews living in a new place may establish a synagogue, school, cemetery, charitable organization, court, or system for caring for people who are poor or sick.

If a community refuses to adapt at all, survival may become difficult. But adapting too completely creates a different problem. If every distinctive tradition disappears, what exactly is being preserved?

questions.stem: Which conclusion about Tuesday's first check-in is best supported by the table?
options: Likud had won the election outright
It showed projections, not results
Yashar would form the government
A bloc had reached 61 seats
questions.exp: "Do not treat polling estimates as actual election results."
why: A tie in polls doesn't show who governs.

questions.stem: Likud had the most seats in the last check-in. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Likud would govern alone with 27 seats
Likud had won a Knesset majority
The election would be repeated at once
Likud still needed partners to govern
questions.exp: Largest party ≠ governing party.

questions.stem: If no bloc reaches 61, what most likely decides who governs?
options: Negotiations with other parties
The president choosing the prime minister alone
A second vote by the public the next day
The party with the most votes automatically
questions.exp: Coalition building after the vote.
why: The president picks who tries, not who wins.
Elections come only if forming a government fails.

questions.stem: A party wins 2.5% of the national vote. What happens?
options: It wins three seats
It joins the government
It wins no seats
It leads the opposition
questions.exp: The threshold is about 3.25%.

questions.stem: After an election, who appoints the person who will try to form a government?
options: The largest party automatically, with no appointment
The Supreme Court of Israel
Israel's president
A vote of all citizens
questions.exp: This was the question you missed on the quick check.
why: Someone must be appointed to try.
Citizens vote for parties, not for who forms the government.

questions.stem: Which statement fits your study guide's description of hostility toward Jews as Jews?
options: Statement 2
Statement 1
Both statements equally
Neither statement
questions.exp: Blaming Jews everywhere for a government's actions targets Jews as Jews.
why: It criticizes a policy and cites reports.
Statement 1 targets a policy, not Jews.
Statement 2 blames Jews as a group.

questions.stem: What makes Statement 1 different from Statement 2?
options: It is louder and more emotional
It mentions Israel's government
It was said out loud at a public protest
It targets a policy and gives evidence
questions.exp: Policy plus evidence vs. a whole people.

questions.stem: Which statement is an overgeneralization?
options: Some people at a protest may hold extreme views
Everyone at a protest holds the same view
A small extremist group can still be dangerous
Protesters' views should be checked with evidence
questions.exp: 'Everyone' turns some into all.

questions.stem: Your review marked 'Most Muslims are Arab' false. What mistake does that statement make?
options: It confuses Israel with Egypt
It confuses an ethnic group with a religion
It confuses the Torah with the Quran
It confuses a government policy with a single person
questions.exp: Arab is an ethnic and language group; Muslim is a religion.
why: It is about group identity, not policy.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the excerpts?
options: Every community used honey on Rosh Hashanah
Rosh Hashanah customs never changed over time in any community
Only Ethiopian Jews kept Rosh Hashanah at all
Communities adapted a shared holiday to local conditions
questions.exp: Shared hope for a sweet year; local forms.
why: Some used sugar; Ethiopian Jews didn't center it.
The excerpts show change and variation.

questions.stem: According to the first excerpt, why weren't apples and honey central to Ethiopian Jewish practice?
options: They developed apart from other communities
Honey was forbidden to Ethiopian Jews by law
They didn't observe Rosh Hashanah at all
Rabbi Chaim Palachi told them to avoid it
questions.exp: Isolation shaped which customs developed.
why: The excerpt gives isolation as the reason.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the author's main point?
options: Physical objects alone can preserve a community
Communities should never change anything
A community needs knowledge, institutions and balance
Communities should adapt completely to fit in with their new neighbors
questions.exp: Knowledge, institutions, and adapting without disappearing.
why: Refusing to adapt makes survival hard.

CAN.title: Canaan
CAN.attr: From the evidence packet "Should He Leave Mesopotamia?" (Source D).
CAN.label: From your class packet.
paras: Unlike southern Mesopotamia, much of Canaan depended heavily on seasonal rainfall rather than a large river-based irrigation system.
Canaan contained towns and fortified settlements as well as rural and pastoral communities.
The region was already inhabited by different groups. Land and water were not simply unclaimed.
Rainfall and harvests could vary from year to year. Drought and famine were serious dangers in the ancient Near East.

G16.label: From your class packet.
paras: Sarai said to Avram, "G-d has kept me from bearing. Consort with my servant; perhaps I shall have a son through her." And Avram listened to Sarai.
He came to Hagar and she conceived; and when she saw that she had conceived, her mistress was lowered in her esteem.
Sarai said to Avram, "The wrong done me is your fault! … Let G-d decide between you and me!"
Avram said to Sarai, "Your servant is in your hands; do to her as you think best." Then Sarai treated her harshly, and Hagar ran away from her.

G22.title: Akeidat Yitzchak (Genesis 22:1–3, 7–8)
G22.attr: Genesis 22, as printed in your Lesson 1.4 source sheet.
G22.label: From your class packet.
paras: G-d tested Avraham and said to him, "Avraham," and he answered, "Here I am." G-d said, "Take your son, your favored one, Yitzchak, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering…"
So early the next morning, Avraham saddled his donkey … and set out for the place of which G-d had told him.

Yitzchak said, "Father! … Here are the firestone and the wood; but where is the sheep for the burnt offering?" Avraham said, "G-d will see to the sheep for the burnt offering, my son." And the two of them walked on together.

SIN.title: Sinai and after (Exodus 19, Exodus 24, Deuteronomy 27)
SIN.attr: As printed in Lesson 2.3 "From Family to Nation."
SIN.label: From your class packet.
paras: "Now, therefore, if you obey my voice faithfully and keep my Covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples … you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." (Exodus 19:5–6)
"All the people answered with one voice, saying: 'Everything that the Lord has spoken we will do' … They said, 'Everything that the Lord has spoken we will do and obey.'" (Exodus 24:3, 7)

"Be silent, Israel, and listen. This day you have become the people of the Lord your G-d. Therefore, obey the Lord your G-d and follow His commandments and decrees." (Deuteronomy 27:9–10, forty years later)

G46.title: Jacob's household (Genesis 46:26–27)
G46.label: From your class packet.
G46.text: All the persons belonging to Jacob who came to Egypt — his own issue aside from the wives of Jacob's sons — all these persons numbered 66. And Joseph's sons who were born to him in Egypt were two in number. Thus the total of Jacob's household who came to Egypt was 70 persons.

EX1.title: A new king (Exodus 1:6–10)
EX1.label: From your class packet.
paras: Joseph died, and all his brothers, and all that generation. But the Israelites were fertile and prolific; they multiplied and increased very greatly, so that the land was filled with them.

A new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph. And he said to his people, 'Look, the Israelite people are far too numerous for us. Let us deal shrewdly with them, so that they may not increase; otherwise in the event of war, they may join our enemies in fighting against us and rise from the ground.'

G47.title: Settling in Goshen (Genesis 45:10; 47:27)
G47.attr: Genesis 45 and 47, as printed in Lesson 2.2.
G47.label: From your class packet.
paras: "You will dwell in the region of Goshen where you will be near me — you and your children and your grandchildren, your flocks and your herds and all that is yours." (45:10)
"Thus Israel settled in the country of Egypt in the region of Goshen; they acquired holdings in it, and were fertile and increased greatly." (47:27)

G50.title: Joseph's last words (Genesis 50:20–25)
G50.label: From your class packet.
G50.text: "Besides, although you intended me harm, G-d intended it for good, so as to bring about the present result — the survival of many people…" So Joseph and his father's household remained in Egypt… At length, Joseph said to his brothers, 'I am about to die. G-d will surely take notice of you and bring you up from this land to the land G-d promised on oath to Abraham, to Isaac and to Jacob.' So Joseph made the sons of Israel swear, saying, 'When G-d has taken notice of you, you shall carry up my bones from here.'

KN.title: Election check-ins
KN.attr: From your Israel Elections 2026 assignment (JTA tracker).
KN.label: From your class packet.
table: Exit polls plus 33% of votes counted

AS.title: Two statements about a protest
AS.attr: Written for practice using the distinction in your study guide.
AS.label: Practice source (written for practice from your class materials; not a verbatim quotation).
paras: Statement 1: "I oppose this Israeli government policy, and here are the reports that explain why."
Statement 2: "Jews everywhere are responsible for what Israel's government does."

WWS.title: What would you save?
WWS.attr: From "What Would You Save? Rebuilding Jewish Life," your two-day assignment.
WWS.label: From your class packet.
paras: A Torah scroll is valuable, but someone must know how to read it. A Jewish calendar identifies holidays, but people must understand how to observe them.

But knowledge alone is not enough. Communities also need institutions. Jews living in a new place may establish a synagogue, school, cemetery, charitable organization, court, or system for caring for people who are poor or sick.

If a community refuses to adapt at all, survival may become difficult. But adapting too completely creates a different problem. If every distinctive tradition disappears, what exactly is being preserved?

questions.stem: Using this source and your evidence packet's description of Canaan, which contrast between Ur and Canaan is best supported?
options: Ur was empty; Canaan was crowded with cities
Ur relied on rivers; Canaan on rain
Ur had no trade; Canaan traded widely
Ur was inhabited; Canaan was unclaimed land
questions.exp: Irrigation vs. seasonal rainfall.
why: Ur was a developed city; Canaan had towns and rural areas.

questions.stem: A student says moving to Canaan was simply a move to free, empty land. Which detail best refutes this?
options: Canaan grew grain, grapes and olives for its towns and villages
Canaan depended on seasonal rainfall
Canaan had coastal plains and valleys
Canaan was already inhabited by different groups
questions.exp: "Land and water were not simply unclaimed."
why: That doesn't address whether land was claimed.

questions.stem: Which detail from this source best helps explain why Yaakov's family later went down to Egypt?
options: Drought and famine were serious dangers
Canaan had fortified settlements
Canaan grew grapes and olives
Routes through Canaan led north and east to other regions
questions.exp: The famine in Joseph's time drove them to Egypt.
why: That doesn't explain going to Egypt.

questions.stem: Which inference is best supported by verse 4 alone?
options: Avram wanted to escape from his father's family in Haran
Avram knew exactly where he was going
Avram responded with obedience, not debate
Avram argued before agreeing to go
questions.exp: The verse records action without discussion.
why: Nothing says he wanted to escape.
The land is 'the land I will show you.'

questions.stem: Which modern example is most like the relationship created in Genesis 12?
options: A boss who gives orders to workers and promises them nothing in return
A person who privately believes something
A mentor and student who each commit to the other
A shopper who buys one item and leaves
questions.exp: A covenant is two-way and ongoing.
why: That is belief, not a two-sided bond.

questions.stem: A classmate says, 'Genesis 12 gives Avram nothing in return for leaving.' Which part of the passage best refutes this?
options: Verses 2 and 3
Verse 1 only
Verse 4 only
The mention of Lot
questions.exp: Verses 2–3 hold the promises.
why: Lot is a companion, not a promise.

questions.stem: How does the palace midrash change our picture of Avraham compared with Genesis 12?
options: He is shown refusing to believe in G-d
He is shown as a king who already owns a great palace
He is shown arguing about Sodom
He is shown searching before G-d speaks
questions.exp: Genesis 12 starts with G-d's call; the midrash starts with Avraham's question.
why: He is the traveler, not the owner.

questions.stem: Which position is best supported by Rambam alone?
options: G-d chose Avraham with no search by him
Avraham took the first step
Avraham learned of G-d from a teacher
Avraham's family taught him one G-d
questions.exp: Position B: Avraham chose G-d.
why: Rambam says he had no teacher.

questions.stem: Which is the best reason a historian might treat Rambam differently from Genesis 12?
options: Rambam contradicts every single detail found in Genesis 12
Rambam interprets the story centuries later
Rambam never mentions Ur or idolaters
Rambam was an eyewitness to Avraham's life
questions.exp: Interpretation vs. the base text.
why: He adds to the story; he doesn't contradict it all.

questions.stem: Based on Genesis 12, the midrash and Rambam together, which position is best supported?
options: Only G-d chose, and Avraham did nothing
Only Avraham chose, and G-d did nothing
Neither chose; Avraham inherited his role
Avraham and G-d chose each other
questions.exp: Each source shows a different side; together they support Position C.
why: Rambam and the midrash show Avraham searching.

questions.stem: Which conclusion about Avraham is best supported by Genesis 13?
options: He gave up an advantage to keep peace
He was afraid of losing a fight with Lot
He wanted the well-watered plain for himself
He disobeyed G-d by separating from Lot
questions.exp: Lot got first choice.

questions.stem: Which pair best shows Avraham acting differently in different situations?
options: Arguing with G-d in Genesis 12; silent before G-d in Genesis 18
Silent in both stories
Silent in Genesis 12; arguing in Genesis 18
Arguing for himself in both
questions.exp: Obedience in one, challenge in the other.

questions.stem: Why is Avraham's argument for Sodom significant for understanding the relationship with G-d?
options: It shows the relationship between them had already ended
It shows Avraham owned Sodom
It shows questioning can be part of it
It shows G-d refused to listen
questions.exp: Your reflection: Judaism leaves room for questioning.
why: He had no claim to Sodom.

questions.stem: Which statement about Avraham in the Hagar story is best supported?
options: He avoided responsibility for the conflict
He protected Hagar from harm
He argued with G-d for Hagar's sake
He ordered Hagar to run away into the wilderness
questions.exp: A weakness, which matters for 'chosen, not perfect.'
why: Sarai treated her harshly and she fled.

questions.stem: Which question best captures the tension between Genesis 18 and Genesis 22?
options: Why Lot left for the Jordan plain
Why Sarai gave Hagar to Avraham
Why Pharaoh feared the Israelites in Exodus chapter 1
Why he argues for strangers but not his son
questions.exp: He challenges G-d for Sodom but rises early to obey at the Akeida.

questions.stem: Using the five stories, which claim about why G-d chose Avraham is strongest?
options: He was chosen because he never made a mistake
He was chosen despite flaws, for his faith and moral courage
He was chosen because he was the richest man
He was chosen only because he always obeyed in silence, never questioning
questions.exp: Strengths and weaknesses both appear.
why: The Hagar story shows a flaw.
Wealth isn't given as a reason.

questions.stem: A student is named team captain and then says, 'Now I never have to listen to anyone.' How does this misunderstand chosenness as your class defined it?
options: Being chosen means you can't make mistakes
Being chosen adds duties, not privileges
Being chosen means nothing at all
Being chosen means only others have duties
questions.exp: Chosenness = responsibility, not superiority or perfection.
why: The chosen one takes on duties.

questions.stem: Which best explains why a covenant is different from personal belief?
options: It requires believing in many gods
It happens only privately, inside a single person's mind
It needs no action from anyone
It creates commitments on both sides
questions.exp: Belief alone doesn't make someone Jewish; the covenant adds obligations.
why: The covenant is with one G-d.

questions.stem: Which order best shows how the covenant develops?
options: Avraham's call → brit milah → Sinai → renewal
Sinai → Avraham's call → brit milah → renewal
Renewal → Sinai → Avraham's call → brit milah
Brit milah → renewal → Avraham's call → Sinai
questions.exp: Individual call, covenant sign, national covenant, renewal by the next generation.

questions.stem: Why does passing righteousness and justice to future generations matter for the covenant?
options: It lets later generations ignore it
It means the covenant ends the moment Avraham himself dies
The covenant lasts only if each generation keeps it
It applies only to Avraham himself
questions.exp: Your notes: responsibility for Avraham and his descendants.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares the covenant with Avraham and the covenant at Sinai?
options: Both were made with the whole people
Both had no conditions at all
One individual first; then a whole people with laws
Sinai replaced Avraham's covenant entirely and erased its promises
questions.exp: Individual vs. national; promise vs. conditions and laws.

questions.stem: What was most significant about 'we will do and obey'?
options: The people committed to act together
The people refused the covenant
Only the leaders agreed
The laws were forced on them against their will
questions.exp: A shared choice that turns a family into a nation.

questions.stem: Someone notices a friend being mocked, says nothing, and later says, 'It wasn't my fault.' What would the Yom Kippur lesson say?
options: Guilty, because they mocked the friend
Not involved at all, since it wasn't theirs
Only responsible if a teacher saw it
Not guilty, but still responsible to act
questions.exp: Guilt ≠ responsibility; noticing isn't acting.
why: Responsibility doesn't depend on being seen.

questions.stem: Which order of generations is correct?
options: Avraham → Yishmael → Yaakov → 12 sons
Avraham → Yitzchak → Yaakov → 12 sons
Yitzchak → Avraham → Yaakov → 12 sons
Avraham → Yaakov → Yitzchak → 12 sons
questions.exp: Jewish lineage runs through Yitzchak and Yaakov.

questions.stem: Joseph and Benjamin share a mother. Who is she?
options: Leah
Rachel
Zilpah
Rivka
questions.exp: Rachel, Yaakov's beloved wife.
why: Leah's sons include Reuben and Judah.
Zilpah's sons are Gad and Asher.

questions.stem: Which detail best supports calling Yaakov's group a family in Genesis 46?
options: It describes them filling the land
It calls them 'the Israelite people'
It describes laws given at Sinai
It counts 70 related persons
questions.exp: Small, related by blood and marriage.

questions.stem: What is the most direct cause of Pharaoh's new attitude toward the Israelites?
options: Their rapid growth in Egypt
Their departure from Goshen
Their acceptance of the Torah
Their alliance with Egypt's enemies
questions.exp: Growth plus a king who 'did not know Joseph.'
why: He fears they might; they haven't.

questions.stem: Which statement is Pharaoh's fear rather than a fact stated in the text?
options: The Israelites multiplied greatly
A new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph
The Israelites would join Egypt's enemies
Joseph and all of his generation died
questions.exp: He says they 'may' join enemies, a fear, not an event.
why: The text states this as fact.

questions.stem: Which pair gives the best practical explanation for staying in Egypt?
options: Slavery and the threat of Pharaoh's army
The Ten Commandments and the Mishkan
Fertile land and Joseph's protection
The Jordan crossing and manna
questions.exp: Goshen was fertile; Joseph had power.

questions.stem: How might Joseph's words have encouraged later generations to remain in Egypt?
options: They could wait for G-d to bring them out
They made Egypt the promised land
They commanded an immediate departure
They told them to fight Pharaoh and take Egypt's land
questions.exp: Pakod yifkod: leaving is on G-d's timing.
why: He names Canaan as the promised land.

questions.stem: Which is something a historian may INFER about why the Israelites stayed in Egypt, rather than what the Torah says?
options: "The iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete"
"G-d will surely take notice of you"
"They acquired holdings and increased"
Economic comfort made leaving unattractive
questions.exp: Torah says / we observe / historians infer.
why: That is what the Torah says.

questions.stem: By Exodus 1, which description of the Israelites is best supported?
options: A family of 70 people
A people, not yet a nation
A nation with land and laws
A kingdom ruling Egypt
questions.exp: Shared history and identity; no land or government.
why: They have no land or laws of their own yet.
They are about to be oppressed.

questions.stem: Which reason best supports ranking the Ten Commandments above manna in creating a nation?
options: Manna happened before the Exodus
Laws gave everyone the same standards
The Ten Commandments ended slavery
Manna was given only to Moshe and the priests
questions.exp: Laws hold a nation together; manna sustained them but added no new feature.

questions.stem: A student claims, 'The Israelites became a nation only when they entered the land.' Which evidence best challenges this?
options: They crossed the Jordan on dry ground
Pharaoh called them far too numerous for Egypt to handle
Genesis counts Yaakov's household as 70 persons
Sinai calls them 'a holy nation' in the wilderness
questions.exp: Exodus 19 and Deuteronomy 27 both speak to them before the land.
why: That shows a people, not nationhood.

questions.stem: Based on the table, which conclusion is best supported?
options: Having the most seats did not mean governing
Likud won a majority of 61 seats
Yashar won the election outright
The poll of polls was the final official election result
questions.exp: Largest party ≠ majority ≠ government.

questions.stem: A coalition of six parties holds 62 seats. One partner with 4 seats quits. What is the most likely result?
options: The government gets stronger
The president takes over
The government may fall
The party that quit becomes largest
questions.exp: Coalitions are fragile.
why: It drops to 58, below a majority.

questions.stem: According to your notes, what happened after World War I that led to outside powers governing the land?
options: Israel declared independence
The Knesset was created
The Ottoman Empire fell
Egypt conquered the region
questions.exp: Ottoman collapse → mandate system.

questions.stem: Which statement is the strongest example of hostility toward Jews as Jews?
options: Statement 2 alone
Statement 1 alone
Both, since both mention Israel
Neither, since both are opinions
questions.exp: Criticism of a government ≠ hostility toward Jews as Jews.
why: It criticizes a policy with evidence.
Mentioning Israel isn't hostility to Jews.
Statement 2 targets Jews as a group.

questions.stem: Which claim from your review is an overgeneralization that was marked false?
options: A small group can pose a serious risk
Both scriptures mention warfare
Some protesters may hold extreme views
All Palestinians are Muslim
questions.exp: 'All' turns some into everyone.

questions.stem: A community moves to a new country and keeps its prayers and school but switches its daily language. Which idea from the reading does this best show?
options: Refusing to adapt to the new country at all
Adapting while preserving what matters
Adapting so completely nothing is left
Depending on one building to survive
questions.exp: The balance between preserving and changing.
why: The reading says Jewish life never depended on one building.
